reference.source: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
clinicalPearls: Erythronychia denotes red discolouration of the nail, seen most usefully as one or more longitudinal red bands running from the lunula to the free edge.

Longitudinal erythronychia reflects a thinned ventral nail plate overlying a vascular focus, often accompanied by distal splinter haemorrhage, a V-shaped nick or subungual keratosis at the free margin.

Single-band (monodactylous) longitudinal erythronychia in one nail should prompt concern for a localised tumour, classically onychopapilloma, but also glomus tumour, Bowen disease or amelanotic melanoma.
Polydactylous longitudinal erythronychia affecting multiple nails is more often associated with systemic or inflammatory dermatoses such as lichen planus, Darier disease or graft-versus-host disease.
Darier disease characteristically produces alternating longitudinal red and white bands with distal wedge-shaped nicking.
Dermoscopy and, where a single symptomatic or evolving band exists, matrix and bed biopsy are central to excluding neoplasia.
A painful single red band, particularly with cold sensitivity and pinpoint tenderness, suggests a glomus tumour.
Because a solitary band can harbour malignancy, persistent monodactylous erythronychia should not be dismissed as cosmetic.
reference.pathophysiology: The red colour is produced when the nail bed vasculature becomes more visible through a nail plate that has been focally thinned or has lost its normal attachment. In localised longitudinal erythronychia a discrete lesion in the distal matrix or bed, such as an onychopapilloma or glomus tumour, alters keratinisation so that the overlying plate is thinned along a narrow channel, allowing the dilated capillaries of the bed to show through as a red line; fragility of this channel accounts for the associated splinter haemorrhages and distal notch. In polydactylous disease a generalised inflammatory or dyskeratotic matrix process, as in lichen planus or Darier disease, produces the same thinning across several nails. The band is therefore a window onto matrix and bed pathology rather than a primary vascular abnormality.
additionalDifferentials: Bowen disease or squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the nail unit
additionalInvestigations: Dermoscopy of the nail plate and free edge
Nail matrix and bed biopsy of a solitary or symptomatic band
Examination of all twenty nails to distinguish mono- from polydactylous disease
Skin and mucosal examination for lichen planus or Darier disease
Imaging such as MRI for suspected glomus tumour
Histopathology of the free-edge subungual keratosis
redFlags: A single persistent or evolving red band, especially if painful or bleeding
Associated nail plate destruction, ulceration or a distal nodule
Rapid change in width, colour or symptoms of a longitudinal band
Erythronychia with a subungual mass or bony change on imaging
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends entirely on the cause: benign onychopapilloma and inflammatory dermatoses do well, whereas an unrecognised subungual carcinoma or melanoma carries the prognosis of the underlying malignancy. Solitary bands therefore merit histological clarification.
pitfalls: Dismissing a solitary longitudinal red band as trivial and missing an underlying tumour
Attributing all erythronychia to systemic disease without examining the individual band morphology
Overlooking a glomus tumour as a cause of an exquisitely tender red streak
Failing to sample the free-edge keratosis, which often holds the diagnostic clue
